title: Τληπόλεμος
about: Fate sets Tlepolemus, a son of Heracles, against Sarpedon, a son of Zeus, and Tlepolemus opens with a taunt: Sarpedon is no true son of Zeus, and his heart is base, whereas Heracles once sacked Troy with six ships. Sarpedon answers that Heracles took Troy only through Laomedon’s folly, and promises Tlepolemus death. They cast together: Tlepolemus dies of a spear through the neck, and Sarpedon takes a spear in the thigh, which his men are too hurried to pull out. Odysseus, who might have gone after Sarpedon, is turned by Athena toward the Lycians and kills seven. Hector comes, and Sarpedon begs not to be left to the Danaans; Hector rushes past him, and his companions lay him under Zeus’s oak, where Pelagon draws out the spear and the North Wind revives him. Under Ares and Hector the Argives give ground, and Hera, seeing it, calls on Athena to act.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν πονέοντο κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην·
sentences.l: So these were toiling in strong battle;
sentences.i: So these men were toiling in strong battle;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν ‘these’ are the rank and file of both armies, set against the pair of champions who step out in the next line. πονέοντο is the imperfect of πονέομαι ‘toil’, with the uncontracted epic ending -έοντο (Attic -οῦντο). κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην, ‘strong battle’, is a stock phrase. The line is the same as one already published, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
Τληπόλεμον δ’ Ἡρακλεΐδην ἠΰν τε μέγαν τε
ὦρσεν ἐπ’ ἀντιθέῳ Σαρπηδόνι μοῖρα κραταιή.
sentences.l:
And Tlepolemus, Heracles’-son, both good and great,
roused against godlike Sarpedon strong fate.
sentences.i: Strong fate roused Tlepolemus, the son of Heracles, both good and great, against godlike Sarpedon.
sentences.n: Tlepolemus, a son of Heracles, and Sarpedon, a son of Zeus, are about to fight, and the poet gives the cause as μοῖρα κραταιή ‘strong fate’, which stands last in the sentence as the subject. Ἡρακλεΐδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Heracles’, and ἠΰν is the epic form of ἐΰν, accusative of ἠΰς ‘good’; ἠΰν τε μέγαν τε is ‘both good and great’. ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, and ἀντιθέῳ, ‘godlike’, is the stock epithet of heroes (ἀντί ‘equal to’ + θεός).

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες
υἱός θ’ υἱωνός τε Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο,
τὸν καὶ Τληπόλεμος πρότερος πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.l:
And when they were near, going against one another,
son and grandson of cloud-gatherer Zeus,
to him also Tlepolemus first spoke a word:
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, the son and grandson of Zeus who gathers the clouds, Tlepolemus was the first to speak a word to him:
sentences.n: The two men are ‘son and grandson of Zeus’: Sarpedon is Zeus’s son, and Tlepolemus his grandson, since Heracles is Zeus’s son. In the last line τὸν ‘him’ is Sarpedon, and πρότερος ‘first’ goes with Τληπόλεμος. καί is ‘also’ in l and adds little here. νεφεληγερέταο has the epic genitive -αο (Attic -ου), and the first line (5.630) stands in a published part, whose English is kept.

sentences.t:
Σαρπῆδον Λυκίων βουληφόρε, τίς τοι ἀνάγκη
πτώσσειν ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντι μάχης ἀδαήμονι φωτί;
sentences.l:
“Sarpedon, counsel-bearer of the Lycians, what need is there for you
to cower here, a man ignorant of battle?
sentences.i: “Sarpedon, counsellor of the Lycians, what need is there for you to cower here, a man ignorant of battle?
sentences.n: Tlepolemus opens with an insult. βουληφόρε, ‘counsel-bearer’, is a title of respect for a leader who sits in council, and in this mouth it sets the man of counsel against the fighter, as the rest of the question shows. τίς τοι ἀνάγκη is ‘what need is there for you’, and the infinitive πτώσσειν ‘to cower’ depends on it. ἐόντι is the dative participle of εἰμί, agreeing with τοι ‘for you’, with φωτί ‘man’ in apposition to it, and μάχης is the genitive of what he is ignorant of.

sentences.t:
ψευδόμενοι δέ σέ φασι Διὸς γόνον αἰγιόχοιο
εἶναι, ἐπεὶ πολλὸν κείνων ἐπιδεύεαι ἀνδρῶν
οἳ Διὸς ἐξεγένοντο ἐπὶ προτέρων ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.i: They are lying when they say that you are the offspring of aegis-bearing Zeus, since you fall far short of those men who were born of Zeus in the time of earlier men;
sentences.n: ψευδόμενοι ‘lying’ is a nominative participle that goes with the unnamed ‘they’ of φασι ‘they say’; Tlepolemus is saying that the claim of Zeus’s fatherhood is false. ἐπιδεύεαι is ‘you lack’, ‘you fall short of’, with the genitive κείνων ἀνδρῶν, and has the epic uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ). ἐξεγένοντο is the aorist of ἐκγίγνομαι ‘be born of’, and ἐπὶ προτέρων ἀνθρώπων is ‘in the time of earlier men’, that is, men of earlier generations.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οἷόν τινά φασι βίην Ἡρακληείην
εἶναι, ἐμὸν πατέρα θρασυμέμνονα θυμολέοντα·
sentences.l:
but such as they say the might of Heracles was,
my father, bold-abiding, lion-hearted;
sentences.i: but such a man as they say the might of Heracles was, my father, bold in standing firm, lion-hearted;
sentences.n: The sentence is left unfinished: the thought to supply is ‘you are not that kind of man’. βίην Ἡρακληείην, ‘the might of Heracles’, is a periphrasis for Heracles himself, and φασι εἶναι is ‘they say … was’. θρασυμέμνονα is built on θρασύς ‘bold’ and μέμνω ‘stay, stand firm’, the second part probably, and θυμολέοντα on θυμός ‘heart’ and λέων ‘lion’; both agree with πατέρα.

sentences.t:
ὅς ποτε δεῦρ’ ἐλθὼν ἕνεχ’ ἵππων Λαομέδοντος
ἓξ οἴῃς σὺν νηυσὶ καὶ ἀνδράσι παυροτέροισιν
Ἰλίου ἐξαλάπαξε πόλιν, χήρωσε δ’ ἀγυιάς·
sentences.i: who once came here for the sake of Laomedon’s horses, with only six ships and fewer men, and plundered the city of Ilios and left its streets widowed;
sentences.n: ὅς is Heracles. Laomedon, king of Troy, is the man whose horses were the cause; Sarpedon’s answer tells the story from his side (648–651). ἕνεχ’ is ἕνεκα ‘for the sake of’, elided, and οἴῃς, ‘alone’, goes with ἓξ … νηυσί ‘with only six ships’. ἐξαλάπαξε is ‘plundered utterly’, and χήρωσε δ’ ἀγυιάς, ‘widowed the streets’, means that the war left the city’s streets full of widows. Ἰλίου is the genitive of the city’s name, and πόλιν ‘city’ is the object.

sentences.t: σοὶ δὲ κακὸς μὲν θυμός, ἀποφθινύθουσι δὲ λαοί.
sentences.l: but to you the heart is base, and the people are wasting away.
sentences.i: but your heart is base, and your people are dying off.
sentences.n: κακός of a man in battle is ‘base’, that is cowardly or without worth. θυμός here is the heart as seat of courage. ἀποφθινύθουσι is ‘waste away, perish’, a present plural, and λαοί ‘people’ are the Lycians whom Sarpedon leads. Tlepolemus is claiming that Sarpedon’s weakness is costing his men their lives.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε Τρώεσσιν ὀΐομαι ἄλκαρ ἔσεσθαι
ἐλθόντ’ ἐκ Λυκίης, οὐδ’ εἰ μάλα καρτερός ἐσσι,
ἀλλ’ ὑπ’ ἐμοὶ δμηθέντα πύλας Ἀΐδαο περήσειν.
sentences.l:
And I do not suspect that you will be any defence to the Trojans,
coming from Lycia, not even if you are very strong,
but, subdued under me, will pass the gates of Hades.”
sentences.i: And I do not suspect that you will be any defence to the Trojans now that you have come from Lycia, not even if you are very strong, but that, overcome by me, you will pass through the gates of Hades.”
sentences.n: The sentence is οὐδέ τί σε ὀΐομαι … ἔσεσθαι ‘nor do I suspect that you will be’, followed by ἀλλά and a second infinitive, περήσειν ‘will pass’, which has to be taken with σε again. ἄλκαρ is a rare noun, ‘defence, protection’, from the root of ἀλκή ‘might’. ἐλθόντ’ is the aorist participle ‘having come’, elided, and καρτερός is the epic form of κρατερός ‘strong’. δμηθέντα is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’; ὑπ’ ἐμοί, with the dative, is ‘under me, at my hands’. Ἀΐδαο has the epic genitive -αο, ‘of Hades’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Σαρπηδὼν Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: Him then in turn Sarpedon, leader of the Lycians, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Sarpedon, leader of the Lycians, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is the reply-formula that brings in the second speaker. αὖ is ‘in turn’, and ἀντίον ηὔδα ‘spoke face to face’; ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’, with the augment ηὐ-. Λυκίων ἀγός is ‘leader of the Lycians’.

sentences.t:
Τληπόλεμ’ ἤτοι κεῖνος ἀπώλεσεν Ἴλιον ἱρὴν
ἀνέρος ἀφραδίῃσιν ἀγαυοῦ Λαομέδοντος,
sentences.l:
“Tlepolemus, that man indeed destroyed sacred Ilium
through the follies of a noble man, Laomedon,
sentences.i: “Tlepolemus, that man did indeed destroy sacred Ilium, through the folly of noble Laomedon,
sentences.n: Sarpedon turns the taunt about: Heracles took Troy because of Laomedon’s fault, not because of his own prowess. κεῖνος is ‘that man’, Heracles, and ἤτοι ‘indeed’ is printed as one word in this edition. Ἴλιον ἱρήν ‘sacred Ilium’ is a stock phrase for Troy. ἀφραδίῃσιν is the epic dative plural of ἀφραδίη ‘folly’, in the plural ‘follies’, and ἀνέρος ἀγαυοῦ Λαομέδοντος is ‘of a noble man, Laomedon’, the genitive depending on it.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥά μιν εὖ ἕρξαντα κακῷ ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ,
οὐδ’ ἀπέδωχ’ ἵππους, ὧν εἵνεκα τηλόθεν ἦλθε.
sentences.l:
who rebuked him with an evil word, when he had done him well,
and did not give back the horses, for whose sake he had come from far away.
sentences.i: and who rebuked Heracles with a cruel word, though Heracles had done him good, and did not give back the horses for whose sake Heracles had come from far away.
sentences.n: Who does what needs care here: ὅς is Laomedon, μιν ‘him’ is Heracles, and Heracles is also the subject of ἦλθε ‘had come’; i supplies the names for that reason. εὖ ἕρξαντα is ‘having done well by’, the aorist participle of ἕρδω ‘do’ with the adverb εὖ. ἠνίπαπε is ‘rebuked’, with κακῷ μύθῳ ‘with an evil word’. ἀπέδωχ’ is ἀπέδωκε ‘gave back’, elided, and ὧν εἵνεκα is ‘for whose sake’, with εἵνεκα = ἕνεκα.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ἐγὼ ἐνθάδε φημὶ φόνον καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν
ἐξ ἐμέθεν τεύξεσθαι, ἐμῷ δ’ ὑπὸ δουρὶ δαμέντα
εὖχος ἐμοὶ δώσειν, ψυχὴν δ’ Ἄϊδι κλυτοπώλῳ.
sentences.i: And I say that here slaughter and the black spirit of death will come upon you from me, and that, overcome under my spear, you will give me the triumph and your soul to Hades of the famous horses.”
sentences.n: φημί takes an accusative and infinitive: φόνον καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν … τεύξεσθαι is ‘that slaughter and black death-fate will be brought about’, with τεύξεσθαι the future middle infinitive of τεύχω ‘make’, passive in sense, and σοί ‘for you’. The second infinitive, δώσειν ‘will give’, has σέ ‘you’ as its subject, understood, and δαμέντα, ‘subdued’, agrees with it. κήρ is the spirit of death, not κῆρ ‘heart’. εὖχος is the thing one boasts of, here the triumph. κλυτοπώλῳ is ‘of the famous horses’, from κλυτός ‘famous’ and πῶλος ‘foal, horse’; why Hades is so called is not known.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο Σαρπηδών, ὃ δ’ ἀνέσχετο μείλινον ἔγχος
Τληπόλεμος·
sentences.l:
So spoke Sarpedon, and he raised the ashen spear,
Tlepolemus;
sentences.i: So spoke Sarpedon, and Tlepolemus raised his ashen spear;
sentences.n: The speeches are over and the fight begins. ὃ δ’ is Tlepolemus, named in apposition at the start of the next line. ἀνέσχετο is the aorist middle of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’. μείλινον is the adjective from μελίη ‘ash’, so ‘of ash-wood’; the ash was the usual wood for spear shafts.

sentences.t:
καὶ τῶν μὲν ἁμαρτῇ δούρατα μακρὰ
ἐκ χειρῶν ἤϊξαν·
sentences.l:
and of both of them the long spears together
darted from their hands;
sentences.i: and the long spears of both flew from their hands at the same moment;
sentences.n: τῶν μέν is ‘of the two’, a genitive that goes with δούρατα ‘spears’. ἁμαρτῇ is an adverb, ‘together, at the same moment’. ἤϊξαν is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, rush’, with the plural verb after a neuter plural subject.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν βάλεν αὐχένα μέσσον
Σαρπηδών, αἰχμὴ δὲ διαμπερὲς ἦλθ’ ἀλεγεινή·
sentences.l:
he indeed hit the middle of the neck,
Sarpedon, and the point went right through, grievous;
sentences.i: Sarpedon hit him in the middle of the neck, and the grievous point went right through;
sentences.n: ὃ μέν ‘he’ is Sarpedon, named after the verb in apposition. αὐχένα μέσσον is the accusative of the part struck: Tlepolemus’ neck. διαμπερές ‘right through’ is an adverb, and ἀλεγεινή ‘grievous’ goes with αἰχμή ‘point’. βάλεν is the aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ἐρεβεννὴ νὺξ ἐκάλυψε.
sentences.l: and over his eyes the murky night covered him.
sentences.i: and murky night covered him over his eyes.
sentences.n: τόν is Tlepolemus, struck through the neck; the line is a stock way of saying that a man dies. ἐρεβεννή ‘murky, dark’ is built on Ἔρεβος ‘darkness’. κατ’ ὀφθαλμῶν is ‘down over his eyes’, with the genitive, and ἐκάλυψε is the aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’.

sentences.t:
Τληπόλεμος δ’ ἄρα μηρὸν ἀριστερὸν ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ
βεβλήκειν, αἰχμὴ δὲ διέσσυτο μαιμώωσα
ὀστέω ἐγχριμφθεῖσα, πατὴρ δ’ ἔτι λοιγὸν ἄμυνεν.
sentences.l:
And Tlepolemus had hit the left thigh with his long spear,
and the point darted through, raging,
grazing the bone, but his father still warded off ruin.
sentences.i: And Tlepolemus had hit him on the left thigh with his long spear, and the point darted through, raging, grazing the bone, but his father still warded off ruin.
sentences.n: Sarpedon’s wound, set beside Tlepolemus’ death, is a lesser one. βεβλήκειν is the pluperfect ‘had hit’, with the epic ending -ειν, and ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ is the dative of means, ‘with the long spear’. μαιμώωσα ‘raging’ is the participle of μαιμάω ‘be eager, rage’, and ἐγχριμφθεῖσα, the aorist passive participle of ἐγχρίμπτω, ‘grazing’; both describe the point. ‘His father’ is Zeus, and λοιγὸν ἄμυνεν is ‘warded off ruin’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἀντίθεον Σαρπηδόνα δῖοι ἑταῖροι
ἐξέφερον πολέμοιο·
sentences.l:
These then, godlike Sarpedon, his heavenly companions
were bearing out of the war;
sentences.i: His heavenly companions then were bearing godlike Sarpedon out of the war;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ‘these then’ are the companions of Sarpedon, δῖοι ἑταῖροι, set in apposition after the object; the same whole line is repeated at 692, with the same English. ἀντίθεον ‘godlike’ is the stock epithet. ἐξέφερον is the imperfect of ἐκφέρω ‘carry out’, and πολέμοιο is the genitive of separation, ‘out of the war’.

sentences.t:
βάρυνε δέ μιν δόρυ μακρὸν
ἑλκόμενον·
sentences.l:
and the long spear weighed on him,
being dragged along;
sentences.i: and the long spear, trailing from him, weighed on him;
sentences.n: μιν ‘him’ is Sarpedon, and βάρυνε is the imperfect of βαρύνω ‘weigh down’. ἑλκόμενον is the passive participle ‘being dragged’, agreeing with δόρυ, the spear still stuck in his thigh and trailing on the ground as he was carried.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν οὔ τις ἐπεφράσατ’ οὐδὲ νόησε
μηροῦ ἐξερύσαι δόρυ μείλινον ὄφρ’ ἐπιβαίη
σπευδόντων·
sentences.i: No one thought of it, nor had the wit to pull the ashen spear out of his thigh so that he could walk, in their haste;
sentences.n: τὸ μέν ‘this’ is the object of both verbs, ἐπεφράσατ’ ‘took thought of’ and νόησε ‘noticed’, and the infinitive ἐξερύσαι ‘to draw out’ explains what ‘this’ is. ὄφρ’ ἐπιβαίη, an aorist optative of purpose from ἐπιβαίνω, is ‘so that he could step’, that is, walk on the leg; the Greek has no object, and l adds ‘it’ to complete the English. σπευδόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘they being in haste’.

sentences.t: τοῖον γὰρ ἔχον πόνον ἀμφιέποντες.
sentences.l: for such toil they had, busying themselves about him.
sentences.i: for they had such toil, busying themselves about him.
sentences.n: τοῖον ‘such’ goes with πόνον ‘toil’, and ἀμφιέποντες is the participle of ἀμφιέπω ‘busy oneself about’; the toil is that of tending to Sarpedon in the press of battle. This is the reason given for the neglect of the spear.

sentences.t:
Τληπόλεμον δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐξέφερον πολέμοιο·
sentences.l:
And Tlepolemus, from the other side, the well-greaved Achaeans
were bearing out of the war;
sentences.i: And on the other side the well-greaved Achaeans were bearing Tlepolemus out of the war;
sentences.n: The Achaeans do for the dead Tlepolemus what Sarpedon’s men did for him. Τληπόλεμον is the object, placed first, and ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’. ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’ is the stock epithet of the Achaeans, printed here with the diaeresis, and ἐξέφερον πολέμοιο is the same phrase as at 664, with the same English.

sentences.t:
νόησε δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
τλήμονα θυμὸν ἔχων, μαίμησε δέ οἱ φίλον ἦτορ·
sentences.l:
and heavenly Odysseus noticed,
having an enduring heart, and his dear heart raged within him;
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus noticed, he of the enduring heart, and his heart raged within him;
sentences.n: The subject of νόησε ‘noticed’ is Odysseus, and what he notices, the carrying off of the wounded, is left to be understood. τλήμονα θυμὸν ἔχων is ‘having an enduring heart’, from τλῆναι ‘endure’, the same root as Odysseus’ epithet ‘much-enduring’. μαίμησε is the aorist of μαιμάω ‘be eager, rage’, and οἱ is the dative ‘in him’. The ‘heart’ is θυμός in the first half and ἦτορ in the second, two words for the seat of feeling.

sentences.t:
μερμήριξε δ’ ἔπειτα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμὸν
ἢ προτέρω Διὸς υἱὸν ἐριγδούποιο διώκοι,
ἦ ὅ γε τῶν πλεόνων Λυκίων ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο.
sentences.l:
And then he pondered, in mind and in heart,
whether he should pursue further the son of loud-crashing Zeus,
or should take the life from more of the Lycians.
sentences.i: And then he pondered in his mind and heart whether to pursue the son of loud-crashing Zeus further, or to take the life from more of the Lycians.
sentences.n: Odysseus weighs two choices, put as an indirect question: ἢ … διώκοι ‘whether he should pursue’ and ἦ … ἕλοιτο ‘or should take’. Both are optatives, which stand for the questions he put to himself in the past. ‘The son of Zeus’ is Sarpedon, and προτέρω is the adverb ‘further’. ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο, ‘take the life from’, is the stock phrase for killing. The first line, 5.671, stands in a published part of the Odyssey, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ Ὀδυσσῆϊ μεγαλήτορι μόρσιμον ἦεν
ἴφθιμον Διὸς υἱὸν ἀποκτάμεν ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ·
sentences.l:
And it was not destined for great-spirited Odysseus
to kill the mighty son of Zeus with sharp bronze;
sentences.i: And it was not destined for great-spirited Odysseus to kill the mighty son of Zeus with sharp bronze;
sentences.n: μόρσιμον ἦεν is ‘it was destined’ (ἦεν = ἦν); the infinitive ἀποκτάμεν, the short epic form of ἀποκτεῖναι, is the thing that was not destined. The dative Ὀδυσσῆϊ μεγαλήτορι ‘for great-spirited Odysseus’ has the epic ending -ηϊ and the epithet that goes with his name. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’. The poet says only that fate did not allow it.

sentences.t: τώ ῥα κατὰ πληθὺν Λυκίων τράπε θυμὸν Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: therefore toward the throng of the Lycians Athena turned his heart.
sentences.i: So Athena turned his heart toward the throng of the Lycians.
sentences.n: τώ ῥα is ‘therefore’: because Odysseus could not kill Sarpedon, Athena turned his spirit elsewhere. κατὰ πληθύν is ‘toward the throng’, with the accusative. τράπε is the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’, and θυμόν is the object, ‘heart’ or ‘spirit’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ὅ γε Κοίρανον εἷλεν Ἀλάστορά τε Χρομίον τε
Ἄλκανδρόν θ’ Ἅλιόν τε Νοήμονά τε Πρύτανίν τε.
sentences.l:
There he took Coeranus, and Alastor, and Chromius,
and Alcandrus, and Halius, and Noemon, and Prytanis.
sentences.i: There he killed Coeranus and Alastor and Chromius and Alcandrus and Halius and Noemon and Prytanis.
sentences.n: A list of seven Lycians killed by Odysseus; the Greek gives only their names. εἷλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, which means ‘kill’ when the object is a man, and it governs all seven accusatives. ἔνθ’ is ἔνθα ‘there’, and ὅ γε ‘he’ is Odysseus.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ἔτι πλέονας Λυκίων κτάνε δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l:
And now he would have killed still more of the Lycians, heavenly Odysseus,
if not then sharply had noticed great Hector of the glancing helmet;
sentences.i: And now heavenly Odysseus would have killed still more of the Lycians, had great Hector of the glancing helmet not been quick to notice;
sentences.n: This is a contrary-to-fact pair: καί νύ κ’ ἔτι … κτάνε is ‘and now he would have killed’, with κ’ = κεν marking ‘would’ and κτάνε an aorist without the augment, and εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ … νόησε is ‘if … had not noticed’. ὀξύ is an adverb, ‘sharply’, and here means that Hector was quick to see it. κορυθαίολος, ‘of the glancing helmet’, is the stock epithet of Hector, from κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ
δεῖμα φέρων Δαναοῖσι·
sentences.l:
And he went through the front-fighters, armed with the fire-faced bronze,
bringing terror to the Danaans;
sentences.i: And he went through the foremost fighters, armed with bronze that has the look of fire, bringing terror to the Danaans;
sentences.n: Hector, seeing Odysseus’ slaughter, goes forward through the front rank; Sarpedon’s plea to him comes next. The first line (5.681) stands in a published part, and its English is kept. διὰ προμάχων is ‘through the front-fighters’, the men who fight in the van, and αἴθοπι χαλκῷ is the stock ‘fire-faced bronze’. δεῖμα is ‘terror’, the object of φέρων ‘bringing’, and Δαναοῖσι is the epic dative plural, ‘to the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
χάρη δ’ ἄρα οἱ προσιόντι
Σαρπηδὼν Διὸς υἱός, ἔπος δ’ ὀλοφυδνὸν ἔειπε·
sentences.l:
and Sarpedon, son of Zeus, rejoiced at him as he came up,
and spoke a mournful word:
sentences.i: and Sarpedon, the son of Zeus, was glad to see him coming, and spoke a mournful word:
sentences.n: χάρη is the aorist of χαίρω ‘rejoice’, and οἱ προσιόντι, ‘at him as he came up’, is a dative participle with the dative of the one rejoiced at. Sarpedon is glad to see Hector, and yet what he says is a plea. ἔπος ὀλοφυδνόν is ‘a mournful word’, from ὀλοφύρομαι ‘lament’, and ἔειπε is the aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t:
Πριαμίδη, μὴ δή με ἕλωρ Δαναοῖσιν ἐάσῃς
κεῖσθαι, ἀλλ’ ἐπάμυνον·
sentences.l:
“Priam’s-son, do not now let me, as prey for the Danaans,
lie there, but come to the defence;
sentences.i: “Son of Priam, do not now let me lie here as prey for the Danaans, but come to my defence;
sentences.n: Πριαμίδη is a patronymic in the vocative, ‘son of Priam’: Hector. μὴ … ἐάσῃς is a prohibition with the aorist subjunctive, ‘do not let’, and με … κεῖσθαι is ‘me to lie’. ἕλωρ is ‘prey’, in apposition to με, and Δαναοῖσιν ‘for the Danaans’ is the epic dative plural. ἐπάμυνον is the aorist imperative of ἐπαμύνω ‘come to the defence’.

sentences.t:
ἔπειτά με καὶ λίποι αἰὼν
ἐν πόλει ὑμετέρῃ, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον ἔγωγε
νοστήσας οἶκον δὲ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
εὐφρανέειν ἄλοχόν τε φίλην καὶ νήπιον υἱόν.
sentences.l:
then may life even leave me
in your city, since I was not, it seems, destined,
having returned home to my dear fatherland,
to gladden my dear wife and infant son.”
sentences.i: afterwards let my life even leave me in your city, since it seems I was not destined, having returned home to my dear fatherland, to gladden my dear wife and little son.”
sentences.n: Sarpedon asks to be saved first and to die later, if he must, inside Troy. λίποι is an aorist optative of wish, ‘may it leave’, with αἰών ‘life’ as its subject. ἔμελλον ἔγωγε … εὐφρανέειν is ‘I was destined to gladden’: εὐφρανέειν is the future infinitive with the epic ending -έειν (Attic -εῖν), and νοστήσας, ‘having returned home’, is the aorist participle. The words οἶκον δὲ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν are a stock line-end, ‘home to my dear fatherland’. νήπιον, ‘infant’, here describes a small child.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ,
ἀλλὰ παρήϊξεν λελιημένος ὄφρα τάχιστα
ὤσαιτ’ Ἀργείους, πολέων δ’ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and him not at all addressed Hector of the glancing helmet,
but rushed past, eager that as quickly as possible
he might thrust back the Argives, and take the life from many.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector of the glancing helmet said nothing at all to him, but rushed past, eager to thrust back the Argives as quickly as he could and to take the life from many.
sentences.n: Hector gives no answer and passes Sarpedon by, intent on driving the Argives back. τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη is ‘and he did not address him at all’, and παρήϊξεν is the aorist of παραΐσσω ‘dart past’. λελιημένος, ‘eager’, is followed by ὄφρα τάχιστα, ‘that as quickly as possible’, with the optatives ὤσαιτ’ ‘he might thrust back’ and ἕλοιτο ‘he might take’. πολέων is the epic genitive plural of πολύς, ‘from many’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἀντίθεον Σαρπηδόνα δῖοι ἑταῖροι
εἷσαν ὑπ’ αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς περικαλλέϊ φηγῷ·
sentences.l:
These then, godlike Sarpedon, his heavenly companions
set down beneath the very fair oak of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.i: His heavenly companions then set godlike Sarpedon down beneath the very fair oak of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.n: The first line is the same as 663, and its English is kept. εἷσαν is the aorist of ἵζω in its transitive sense, ‘set down, seat’, and ὑπό with the dative φηγῷ is ‘beneath the oak’. The oak is Zeus’s, and Sarpedon is Zeus’s son. περικαλλέϊ is the dative of περικαλλής ‘very fair’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα οἱ μηροῦ δόρυ μείλινον ὦσε θύραζε
ἴφθιμος Πελάγων, ὅς οἱ φίλος ἦεν ἑταῖρος.
sentences.l:
and out of his thigh the ashen spear pushed, outside,
mighty Pelagon, who was his dear companion.
sentences.i: and mighty Pelagon, who was his dear companion, pushed the ashen spear right out of his thigh.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ὦσε is a verb split in two (tmesis), ‘pushed out’, and θύραζε is ‘outside’, here out through the wound. The subject, ἴφθιμος Πελάγων ‘mighty Pelagon’, comes after the object, and nothing more is told about him. ὅς οἱ φίλος ἦεν ἑταῖρος is ‘who was a dear companion to him’, with ἦεν = ἦν.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἔλιπε ψυχή, κατὰ δ’ ὀφθαλμῶν κέχυτ’ ἀχλύς·
sentences.l: and the soul left him, and over his eyes a haze was poured;
sentences.i: His soul left him, and a haze was poured down over his eyes;
sentences.n: ἔλιπε ψυχή, ‘the soul left him’, is what the poet says of a man who faints, as well as of one who dies; he revives in the next line. κέχυτ’ is the elided pluperfect passive of χέω ‘pour’, ‘was poured’ (the pluperfect gives the state reached), and ἀχλύς is a haze, a mist over the eyes. κατὰ … ὀφθαλμῶν is ‘down over his eyes’.

sentences.t:
αὖτις δ’ ἐμπνύνθη, περὶ δὲ πνοιὴ Βορέαο
ζώγρει ἐπιπνείουσα κακῶς κεκαφηότα θυμόν.
sentences.l:
but again he recovered his breath, and about him the breath of the North Wind
revived, blowing on him, his badly spent-breath spirit.
sentences.i: but he drew breath again, and the breath of the North Wind, blowing about him, revived his grievously exhausted, gasping spirit.
sentences.n: ἐμπνύνθη is the aorist passive of ἐμπνύω ‘recover one’s breath’. πνοιὴ Βορέαο, ‘the breath of the North Wind’, is the cool wind that brings him round, and ζώγρει, an imperfect, is here ‘revive’; the word usually means ‘take alive’. κεκαφηότα is a rare perfect participle whose derivation is disputed, perhaps from an old verb ‘breathe out, gasp’; it stands also at Odyssey 5.468 with the same noun, and the English follows the Odyssey’s: ‘spent-breath’ in l, ‘exhausted, gasping’ in i, with κακῶς ‘badly, grievously’ added. The sense is not certain. It agrees with θυμόν, the spirit as the breath of life.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ὑπ’ Ἄρηϊ καὶ Ἕκτορι χαλκοκορυστῇ
οὔτε ποτὲ προτρέποντο μελαινάων ἐπὶ νηῶν
οὔτε ποτ’ ἀντεφέροντο μάχῃ,
sentences.l:
And the Argives, under Ares and Hector bronze-armed,
neither ever turned toward the black ships
nor ever set themselves against them in battle,
sentences.i: And the Argives, under Ares and Hector armed in bronze, never turned and made for the black ships, nor did they stand up to them in battle,
sentences.n: Under Ares and Hector the Argives neither run to the ships nor hold their ground, so that they fall back. ὑπ’ Ἄρηϊ καὶ Ἕκτορι is ‘under Ares and Hector’, with the dative, and Ares is the god, named plainly at 702. χαλκοκορυστῇ, ‘armed in bronze’, comes from κορύσσω ‘arm’ and is a stock epithet of Hector. προτρέποντο, from προτρέπομαι, is ‘turned forward’, usually taken to mean turned and ran for the ships, and ἀντεφέροντο, from ἀντιφέρομαι, ‘set themselves against’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰὲν ὀπίσσω
χάζονθ’, ὡς ἐπύθοντο μετὰ Τρώεσσιν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l:
but always backward
were giving ground, when they learned Ares was among the Trojans.
sentences.i: but always gave ground backward, once they learned that Ares was among the Trojans.
sentences.n: χάζονθ’ is the imperfect middle χάζοντο ‘were giving ground’, with its last vowel dropped and the τ made θ before the rough breathing of ὡς. ὡς ἐπύθοντο is ‘when they learned’, the aorist of πυνθάνομαι, and Ἄρηα is the accusative subject of an unexpressed ‘was’: ‘learned (that) Ares (was) among the Trojans’, with μετὰ Τρώεσσιν ‘among the Trojans’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα τίνα πρῶτον τίνα δ’ ὕστατον ἐξενάριξαν
Ἕκτωρ τε Πριάμοιο πάϊς καὶ χάλκεος Ἄρης;
sentences.l:
Then whom first, whom last, did they despoil,
Hector, Priam’s son, and bronze Ares?
sentences.i: Whom did they kill and strip of his armour first, and whom last, Hector, the son of Priam, and Ares in bronze?
sentences.n: The poet asks himself who fell first and who last, and then answers with a list of six names; he does not call on the Muse here. ἐξενάριξαν is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘strip of arms’, which also means ‘kill and strip’, and the two subjects are Hector and Ares. Πριάμοιο has the epic genitive -οιο, and πάϊς is παῖς ‘son’. χάλκεος, ‘of bronze’, is the stock epithet of Ares, for the bronze of his armour.

sentences.t:
ἀντίθεον Τεύθραντ’, ἐπὶ δὲ πλήξιππον Ὀρέστην,
Τρῆχόν τ’ αἰχμητὴν Αἰτώλιον Οἰνόμαόν τε,
Οἰνοπίδην θ’ Ἕλενον καὶ Ὀρέσβιον αἰολομίτρην,
sentences.l:
godlike Teuthras, and after him the horse-lashing Orestes,
and Trechus, the Aetolian spearman, and Oenomaus,
and Helenus, Oenops’-son, and Oresbius of the glancing belt,
sentences.i: godlike Teuthras, and after him Orestes the horse-lasher, and Trechus, the Aetolian spearman, and Oenomaus, and Helenus, son of Oenops, and Oresbius of the glancing belt,
sentences.n: The names are all accusatives, the objects of ἐξενάριξαν at 703. ἐπὶ δέ is ‘and after (him)’. πλήξιππον, ‘horse-lashing’, is from πλήσσω ‘strike’ and ἵππος ‘horse’, and αἰχμητήν is ‘spearman’. Οἰνοπίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Oenops’, so this Helenus is not the Trojan seer Helenus, Priam’s son. αἰολομίτρην is ‘of the glancing belt’, from αἰόλος ‘glancing’ and μίτρη, a belt or band worn about the waist.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥ’ ἐν Ὕλῃ ναίεσκε μέγα πλούτοιο μεμηλώς,
λίμνῃ κεκλιμένος Κηφισίδι·
sentences.l:
who in Hyle was dwelling, greatly concerned with wealth,
lying beside the Cephisian lake;
sentences.i: who dwelt in Hyle, greatly concerned with wealth, lying beside the Cephisian lake;
sentences.n: ὅς is Oresbius, the last in the list. ναίεσκε is the iterative imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, with the suffix -σκ- of repeated or habitual action. μέγα πλούτοιο μεμηλώς, ‘greatly concerned with wealth’, has the perfect participle of μέλω with the genitive. κεκλιμένος is ‘lying’, from κλίνω, ‘leaning’ and hence settled, beside the Κηφισίς λίμνη ‘Cephisian lake’.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δέ οἱ ἄλλοι
ναῖον Βοιωτοὶ μάλα πίονα δῆμον ἔχοντες.
sentences.l:
and beside him the other Boeotians
dwelt, having a very rich land.
sentences.i: and beside him dwelt the other Boeotians, who held a very rich land.
sentences.n: πὰρ δέ οἱ is ‘and beside him’, with πάρ = παρά and οἱ the dative ‘him’, Oresbius. The Boeotians are the people of the region around the lake, and δῆμον here is ‘land’, not ‘people’. μάλα πίονα is ‘very rich’, from πίων ‘fat, rich’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη
Ἀργείους ὀλέκοντας ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ,
αὐτίκ’ Ἀθηναίην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And when, then, she noticed them, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
the Argives destroying in strong battle,
at once to Athena winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: And when the goddess, white-armed Hera, then saw them destroying the Argives in strong battle, at once she spoke winged words to Athena:
sentences.n: τοὺς ‘them’ are Hector and Ares, and the participle ὀλέκοντας ‘destroying’ agrees with it, with Ἀργείους as its object. ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε is ‘when, then, she noticed’, and ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ ‘in strong battle’ is a stock phrase. The last line is the formula that introduces a speech, as at 4.69 with Zeus as the subject. The English of that line is kept, with only the pronoun changed to ‘she’, since the speaker is Hera.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος Ἀτρυτώνη,
ἦ ῥ’ ἅλιον τὸν μῦθον ὑπέστημεν Μενελάῳ
Ἴλιον ἐκπέρσαντ’ εὐτείχεον ἀπονέεσθαι,
sentences.l:
“Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone,
truly vain was the word we undertook to Menelaus,
that Ilios, well-walled, having sacked-utterly, he should return home,
sentences.i: “Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone, truly vain was the promise we undertook to Menelaus, that he should sack well-walled Ilios and return home,
sentences.n: Hera reminds Athena of what they promised Menelaus: that he would sack Troy and go home. ὢ πόποι ‘ah’ is an exclamation. Ἀτρυτώνη, ‘Atrytone’, is the vocative of a title of Athena, whose meaning is not known. The first line (5.714) and the last (5.716) stand in published parts (5.714 is Hera’s own address to Athena at 2.157; 5.716 is Agamemnon’s at 2.112), and their English is kept as far as the new subject allows: ‘he’ here where the published 5.716 has ‘I’. ἅλιον ‘vain’ is the predicate of τὸν μῦθον. ἐκπέρσαντ’ is the aorist participle ‘having sacked’, agreeing with the unexpressed ‘he’ of the infinitive ἀπονέεσθαι ‘to return home’, and ὑπέστημεν is the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι ‘undertake’.

sentences.t: εἰ οὕτω μαίνεσθαι ἐάσομεν οὖλον Ἄρηα.
sentences.l: if we shall let ruinous Ares rage so.
sentences.i: if we are going to let ruinous Ares rage like this.
sentences.n: The clause is the condition that makes the promise vain: if Ares is let to rage unchecked, Menelaus cannot take Troy. εἰ … ἐάσομεν is ‘if we shall let’, with the future of ἐάω, and μαίνεσθαι ‘to rage’ is the infinitive that goes with it. οὖλον ‘ruinous’ is the epithet of Ares, as at 5.461.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ καὶ νῶϊ μεδώμεθα θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.l: But come now, let us two also be mindful of impetuous might.”
sentences.i: But come, let us two also be mindful of impetuous might.”
sentences.n: ἄγε δή is ‘come now’, and the exhortation is in the present subjunctive μεδώμεθα ‘let us be mindful’, with the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘of impetuous might’. νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, Hera and Athena. The line is the same as one already published, and its English is kept.
